blocks.text: It is accurate to call the periodic table of elements the symbol of chemistry. It is a vital and thorough source of chemical knowledge and much more than a simple chart; without its systematic categorisation and arrangement of elements it would be difficult to explore and comprehend the enormous area of chemistry. Elements are arranged in the current table by atomic number, electronic configuration and recurring chemical characteristics, which provides the foundation for comprehending the 118 elements and their properties.

Just three centuries ago fewer than a dozen elements were known. By 1700 only 12 were recognised: gold, silver, copper, iron, lead, tin, mercury, phosphorus, sulfur, carbon, zinc and arsenic. As more were discovered, scientists tried to organise them systematically.

items: Antoine Lavoisier, up to the end of the 18th century, attempted to classify the known elements as metals and non-metals.

Dobereiner, in 1829, grouped elements into triads, groups of three with similar properties, noting that the atomic weight of the middle element was roughly the average of the other two; lithium, sodium and potassium are an example.

John Newlands, an English chemist, in 1864 first observed periodicity in the 62 known elements: arranged by increasing atomic mass, every eighth element had similar properties, so he classified them into groups in which every eighth element resembled the first.

Dmitri Mendeleev, a Russian chemist considered the father of the periodic table, in 1869 arranged 63 elements into eight vertical columns by increasing atomic mass, aligning elements with similar properties into vertical groups. The success of his table lay in leaving gaps for undiscovered elements and predicting their atomic masses and properties, which proved accurate when the elements were found.
Lothar Meyer, in the same year, plotted atomic volumes against atomic weights; his curves also showed periodicity.

Moseley, in 1913, determined the exact atomic numbers of the known elements using X-ray emission and arranged the elements by atomic number instead of atomic mass, resolving the flaws in Mendeleev's table. He modified the periodic law to state that the properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.

blocks.title: Mendeleev
blocks.text: Mendeleev arranged the elements by their atomic masses, and his table was the first most notable effort in the classification of elements.

blocks.prompt: Mendeleev left gaps in his table; Moseley later rearranged it. What did each contribution add, and why did Moseley's change remove the flaws?
blocks.explanation: Mendeleev's gaps predicted elements not yet discovered, with their masses and properties, and the predictions came true, which made the table credible. But ordering by atomic mass left some elements out of place. Moseley measured atomic numbers by X-ray emission and ordered the elements by atomic number, so the periodic law became a function of atomic number and the discrepancies disappeared.

items: The periodic table orders the 118 elements by atomic number, electronic configuration and recurring properties.

Lavoisier (metals and non-metals), Dobereiner (triads, 1829), Newlands (every eighth element, 1864), Mendeleev (eight columns by mass with predictive gaps, 1869), Meyer (atomic volume curves) and Moseley (atomic numbers, 1913; periodic law by atomic number).
